From images to coordinates

A photograph depicts an object. Its pixel array records an image. Which relationships survive when we choose a different representation?

1. Color image

Click either image to select an area.

Each 8 × 8 area supplies one value in the reduced image.

2. Grayscale values

3. A vector

The same 784 values, listed in row order. In the code below, x names the pixel vector.

No values are discarded when this 28 × 28 array is flattened. Reducing the original color photograph to grayscale and 28 × 28 does discard information.






Two measurements → two coordinates
Select an image to highlight its point. Adjust its intensity to move it through this space.
Bold x denotes the two-feature vector here; regular italic x₁ and x₂ denote its components. Both axes use intensity units at the same scale.


A deliberately simple image space
x₁: mean intensity.
x₂: RMS contrast: the standard deviation of pixel intensities.
Different images can have similar values on these two measurements. Proximity here need not match similarity of objects.
Coordinates of the displayed 28 × 28 images

Images: course Assignment 1 stimulus bundle, used with Peterson, Abbott & Griffiths (2018). Grayscale conversion and reduction use the existing lecture preparation pipeline. Intensity scaling, rounding and clipping are applied to the reduced image; full-resolution color and grayscale views remain references. Clicking them selects the corresponding 8 by 8 source region, whose averaged grayscale value supplies one reduced pixel. Values shown in the coordinate table are rounded; distances use unrounded coordinates.
